title: CX Digital Media Inc. v. Smoking Everywhere Inc.
lead: An advertising client tells its affiliate network there is no volume limit during an instant-message exchange, and registrations surge. When invoices go unpaid, a bench trial addresses the messages, implementation, corporate authority, and the original signed-modification clause.

actors.name: CX Digital Media
actors.role: Affiliate advertising network that directed and paid for customer traffic.

actors.name: Smoking Everywhere
actors.role: Electronic-cigarette seller promising payment for qualifying registrations.

actors.name: Nick Touris
actors.role: Client’s advertising vice-president who signed the original order and exchanged messages.

actors.name: Pedram Soltani
actors.role: CX Digital account manager arranging the changes.

proceedings: After a five-day bench trial under agreed Delaware law, the court found enforceable modifications and unpaid compensation.
The findings authorized principal, contractual interest, fees, and costs and directed a separately proposed final judgment.
limits: This transforms the canonical trial-opinion brief without a fresh audit or later-law certification. The March 23 opinion directs a later judgment; that judgment is not treated as read. The printed second interest base is preserved despite its $5,000 discrepancy. The established 200-per-day cap and September 2, 2009 exchange control over contradictory isolated printed dates or figures.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The original insertion order pays for registrations, not retained products
sections.cue: What obligations existed before the messages?
paragraphs: CX Digital Media ran an affiliate advertising network that sent prospective buyers to Smoking Everywhere’s electronic-cigarette offer. Tracking software counted a contractual Sale when a credit-card submission succeeded and the customer reached a confirmation page, without requiring proof that the customer ultimately retained or paid for a delivered product. CX Digital owed its affiliates even if the client did not pay.

On August 4, 2009, Smoking Everywhere’s advertising vice-president Nick Touris signed insertion order 6921 at $45 per qualifying registration, limited to 200 daily and specified destination URLs. August generated 670 Sales without exceeding the daily cap. The $30,150 charge less a $5,000 deposit left $25,150 due September 15.

sections.title: A day-long exchange changes pages and volume
sections.cue: What did Touris’s response accept, and what did it omit?
paragraphs: On September 2, Touris and CX Digital manager Pedram Soltani arranged two new landing pages, tracking pixels, and link tests through instant messages. Later Soltani requested roughly 2,000 daily orders and an agent-of-record arrangement granting exclusivity. Touris replied that there was no limit. Soltani responded enthusiastically, and affiliates immediately increased performance.

Between September 2 and 23, average daily Sales reached about 1,244, peaking at 2,896 on September 22. On September 10, the client objected to affiliates describing the offer as free and other advertised terms; Soltani directed compliance. It did not then demand the original URLs or cap.

CX Digital removed the offer around September 23–24 for nonpayment. Promised October payment failed, and an October 7 identity-fraud complaint arrived after affiliates had been paid. A September invoice used $51 for some Sales, but CX Digital abandoned the six-dollar increase at trial and sought $45 throughout.

sections.title: The court finds narrow modifications from words and implementation
sections.cue: Why was the volume response a counteroffer?
paragraphs: After a five-day bench trial, Judge Cecilia Altonaga applied the parties’ agreed Delaware law. Original validity was conceded. Smoking Everywhere disputed authorization, assent, formality, consideration, authority, and various performance defenses.

The new-page agreement appeared objectively in Touris’s installation and testing work and later informed advertising complaints. His private understanding could not negate implemented conduct, and agreement did not require identification of one precise formation instant. An unclear tracking objection did not prove customer fraud.

The volume reply was not literal acceptance of Soltani’s two-part proposal: it authorized unlimited volume without exclusivity. It was a counteroffer accepted by reply and immediate performance. Days exceeding 2,000 confirmed no replacement ceiling at that figure. Intermittent office responses within the day-long conversation did not cause lapse, and no persuasive alternative topic explained Touris’s response. The interval might have allowed internal approval, but the court did not find approval occurred.

Unlike vague revisions to complex bargains, these changes were limited and documented by messages and performance. The messages supplied a written record, but the holding did not require finding electronic signatures. Because the contract concerned services, Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209’s goods rule did not apply.

sections.title: Waiver, reliance, consideration, and apparent authority answer enforcement defenses
sections.cue: Why did the signed-writing clause not control the outcome?
paragraphs: Under the Delaware common-law rule applied, parties could waive a signed-modification requirement by subsequent agreement or conduct, as implementation showed here. No statute of frauds independently required signed changes; such an affirmative defense also had not been pleaded. This was not a universal holding that instant messages meet all signature requirements.

Alternatively, Smoking Everywhere’s participation and accepted performance supported estoppel after CX Digital materially changed position by directing and paying affiliates. That was an enforcement rationale rather than a separately adjudicated promissory-estoppel cause. Increased Sales exchanged for existing-rate payments supplied volume consideration. Changed URLs supplied none independently, but material reliance supported enforcement under Restatement § 89. Failure to make a proposed $20,000 deposit would concern breach of that promise, not absence of consideration.

Touris had apparent authority: the company presented him as its advertising vice-president, let him sign the original order, and had him implement changes. Reliance was reasonable. The judge rejected a late assertion that Soltani knew further approval was always required, including additional testimony admitted after closing arguments, because it conflicted with earlier evidence and counsel’s opening account. This did not confer unlimited power on every vice-president or find actual chief-executive approval. A later insertion order excluded for discovery misconduct did not undo prior modifications.

sections.title: Fraud and other theories do not justify withholding payment
sections.cue: What performance had the client purchased?
paragraphs: The fraud clause required prompt, particular documentation of disputed Sales within five days. No August Sales were timely challenged, and later accusations supplied no contractual withholding basis. Smoking Everywhere received the qualifying registrations it had agreed to purchase.

The court rejected frustration and an implied-duty theory aimed at conduct the modified bargain authorized. Mutual mistake likewise failed: the client identified no shared material misconception at formation and continued to describe the original cap and URLs as knowingly chosen. Disagreement about later modification did not establish an original mistake.

sections.title: The findings calculate principal and direct a later judgment
sections.cue: What figures did the opinion actually state?
paragraphs: At $45 each, 670 August Sales yielded $30,150 and 27,459 later Sales yielded $1,235,655. Less the $5,000 deposit, principal totaled $1,260,805. The court also authorized contractual attorney’s fees, costs, and monthly interest of 1.5 percent.

It stated interest on $25,150 from September 15, 2009 and on a further $1,240,655 from October 15. That second printed base exceeds remaining principal after the August balance by $5,000; the opinion’s stated figure is preserved rather than silently recalculated.

The March 23, 2011 findings directed CX Digital to propose a final judgment by March 30 for entry separately. They did not themselves supply the unread later judgment’s terms. Altonaga issued the sole trial writing, with no separate opinion or vote.
